requested.title: Server-island endpoint renders any island with no authorization and no `handle` middleware; prop-less islands need no sealed token
Form-action dispatch resolves `Object.prototype` members, yielding forged `form.ok: true` renders and unauthenticated 500s
SSE frame builder splits only on `\n`, so a CR in `data` (or any newline in `id`/`event`) injects forged events into the stream
WebSocket upgrades are accepted with no Origin validation (cross-site WebSocket hijacking)
`/__mochi/health/memory` is unauthenticated, has no `development` guard, and forces a blocking full GC per request
publicDir files are raw Bun static routes, so `handle` middleware (auth, security headers) never runs for them — contradicting the docs
Svelte compile errors (absolute paths and code frames) are rendered to clients in production
Highlighter memo cache is bounded by entry count, not bytes, with no TTL — unbounded retention for apps highlighting user content
MOCHI_KEY fails open: a non-base64url value decodes to 0 bytes, making every sealed token forgeable
`request`/`error` event `path` carries the query string despite being documented as the pathname, leaking URL-borne tokens to logs and metrics sinks
`hasSubscribers()` ignores mitt wildcard subscribers, so gated events are dropped for `on('*')` listeners
Cron reconcile deletes every undeclared schedule in shared cron storage, so a dev boot silently unschedules production `dev: false` jobs
`Mochi.worker().stop()` never clears `started`, so a stopped worker cannot be restarted

parsedVerdicts.reasoning: Verified end-to-end. `bunRoutes[`${assetPrefix}/island/:componentName`]` (Mochi.ts:1559) calls `buildRequestContext(req, server, { kind: 'island' })`, and `KIND_POLICY.island` in runtime/requestSetup.ts:67 is `{ timeout: false, trailingSlash: false, csrf: false, debugBar: false }`. `middleware` is invoked at exactly three sites in Mochi.ts — 991 (page), 1240 (api), 1922 (composedFetch/assets) — and nowhere in the island handler; `resolveLimiter`/`checkRouteLimit` likewise only run in the `isMochiPage`/`isMochiApi` branches, so the endpoint has no rate limit either. Only the `protection` PoW gate (cfg.protection, requestSetup.ts:130) and the `serverIslandPaths` membership check apply. Lines 1574-1586 confirm `if (signedProps) {decrypt} else {decodedProps = {}}` — an absent token is treated as 'no props', not as a missing capability, so `GET /_mochi/island/<key>` renders the island with `props={}`, empty `locals`, and no authz. The docs make this a genuine trap: types.ts:528 says `handle` wraps 'every incoming request — authentication, logging, headers'; docs/120-middleware.md's `event.kind` table lists only page/api/asset/fallback/error and documents only WS/SSE as middleware-exempt; and docs/70-server-islands.md:222 actively tells authors to 'fetch data inside the island' via `getRequestContext()` rather than through props — exactly the shape that leaks when the render runs unauthenticated. One correction to the finding: the claim that prop-less islands routinely hit this branch is wrong. svelteAstPreprocess.ts:295-318 always injects `islandId: __mochi_iid` into the envelope, so every emitted `<mochi-server-island>` carries a `signed-props` attribute ('Server islands always emit signed-props') — the empty-props branch is reachable only by a hand-crafted request. That does not weaken the vulnerability (the server still does not require the token), only the 'mainstream path' framing. Discoverability is a real but surmountable obstacle: the key is `<localName>_<base36 Bun.hash(project-relative path)>` (islandIdentity, line 492), an unkeyed deterministic hash the code comment confirms is stable across machines, so it is computable offline from a guessed source path and visible in the HTML of any page that uses the island. Keeping HIGH: conditional on app shape (authz in `handle` + a defer island that doesn't read `locals`), but a real confused-deputy with no framework-side mitigation and no documentation of the exemption.

The mechanism is exactly as described. Mochi.ts:1051-1056 derives `actionName` from the first `/`-prefixed query key with no charset validation, then line 1057 does `const actionHandler = livePostActions[actionName]`, and `MochiFormActions = Record<string, MochiFormActionHandler>` (types.ts:153) is in practice an object literal, so the lookup walks the prototype chain. `?/constructor` resolves to `Object` — truthy, so the 404 branch at 1058 is skipped — and `Object(eventObject)` returns the event object, which is not a `Response`, not `isRedirect`, not `isFormFail`, not `isFormSuccess`, so execution falls through to 1165-1167: `ctx.form = { ok: true, action: 'constructor', data: {} }` plus `emitActionComplete(..., 'success')` and a 200 re-render (or `{type:'success'}` JSON on the enhance path). `?/__proto__` resolves to `Object.prototype`, which is truthy but not callable, so `await actionHandler(...)` throws a TypeError caught at 1115 and turned into a 500 error page. The repo's prior art is exactly where the finding says: image/config.ts:164-166 uses `Object.hasOwn(options.sizes, name)` with the comment about 'prototype-chain hits like "constructor"', and image/config.test.ts:80-87 asserts it for toString/constructor/hasOwnProperty/__proto__. I repo-wide grepped for `Object.hasOwn`/`__proto__` guards and found none on the action-dispatch path, so it is genuinely unfixed. Downgrading MEDIUM→BUG on impact: `csrfCheck` does block the browser-driven cross-site path (form content types are protected on POST), so a cross-origin page cannot make a victim's browser trigger this; a direct client (curl with a matching Origin) only forges success in its own response. What remains is an unauthenticated forced 500 per request plus bogus `action:complete`/`error` bus events — a real robustness/log-integrity defect, not a cross-privilege vulnerability.

Confirmed in `MochiSseStream.send` (Mochi.ts:1386-1405): `id` and `event` are interpolated with zero validation (`frame += `id: ${opts.id}
``), and the body is split with `data.split('
')` — LF only. The HTML spec's event-stream parser splits lines on CRLF, a lone LF, *or* a lone CR, so `send('hellodata: forged')` puts `data: hellodata: forged

` on the wire, which EventSource parses as two dispatched events ('hello', then 'forged'); a bare `
` in `id`/`event` is even cheaper and lets an attacker set an arbitrary event type or poison `Last-Event-ID`. Nothing downstream normalizes it: the string chunks go straight through `controller.enqueue` into `new Response(body)`. The framework owns the framing (it already splits on `
`, so newline handling was considered and CR was simply missed) and docs/110-server-sent-events.md:39-44 documents `send(data, {event, id})` with no sanitization requirement, so this is squarely a framework defect rather than an app責任. Exploitation requires an app to pass attacker-influenced text into `send` — realistic for a chat/notification feed, and the mitigating detail is that the documented `JSON.stringify(...)` idiom escapes CR as `\r`, so every in-repo SSE route (site/demos streams, queue, admin stock) is immune. Keeping MEDIUM: the primitive is real and the consequence when triggered (forged server-authored events in other users' streams) is meaningful.

Verified. The `Mochi.ws()` handler (Mochi.ts:1262-1328) calls `buildRequestContext(..., { kind: 'ws' })`, and `KIND_POLICY.ws` sets `csrf: false` (requestSetup.ts:66). Even with csrf enabled, `csrfCheckDefault` would pass: it returns `null` unless the method is in `DEFAULT_PROTECTED_METHODS` (POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE) *and* the content type is form-like (csrf.ts:126-131), and a WebSocket handshake is a GET. The handshake then reaches `server.upgrade(req, {...})` at 1310 with the victim's cookies attached and no comparison of `Origin` against `resolveExpectedOrigin()`. The route is matched by Bun's router, so `composedFetch` (the one other `csrfCheck` call site) never sees it either. Browsers apply neither same-origin policy nor preflight to WebSockets, so `new WebSocket('wss://victim/ws/chat')` from any attacker page connects as the logged-in victim with full bidirectional access — textbook cross-site WebSocket hijacking. The documentation steers users straight into it: docs/100-websocket-routes.md:73 says 'Reject unauthenticated sockets in `upgrade`, not `message`', and :81 says 'getRequestContext() works inside `upgrade`, so cookies and getClientAddress() are available there' — cookie auth in `upgrade` succeeds for a cross-origin attacker. The doc's own code sample happens to use a custom header (`x-user-id`), which a browser cannot set on a WS handshake, so the example itself is safe; the hazard is the cookie path the prose advertises. MEDIUM is right: no framework-side mitigation exists, but exploitation depends on the app choosing cookie-based auth in `upgrade`.

Every code claim checks out. Mochi.ts:1816-1823 registers `/__mochi/health/memory` on `process.env.MOCHI_MEMORY_PROBE === '1'` alone, as a bare handler: it does not go through `buildRequestContext`, so neither the protection gate nor middleware nor any rate limiter applies, and it calls `Bun.gc(true)` — a synchronous full collection on Bun's single JS thread — before returning `process.memoryUsage()`. The asymmetry the finding highlights is real: every sibling internal route is `development && …` (`debugBarEnabled` at 503 for buildClientStatsRoutes/buildPageCacheAdminRoutes, `emailViewerEnabled` at 619 for the email viewer), while this one has no mode check at all. Downgrading MEDIUM→BUG on reachability, which I checked rather than assumed: a repo-wide grep shows `MOCHI_MEMORY_PROBE=1` is set in exactly one place — `Dockerfile.memtest:53`, a dedicated memory-regression harness image that runs `NODE_ENV=development` and is described as 'intended for an unattended multi-day run on a dedicated box'. It is not the deploy image (`Dockerfile` / `Dockerfile.production`), appears in no `.env.example`, and the project's own notes list `MOCHI_MEMORY_PROBE` among the flag-gated dev surfaces. So the finding's 'plausible for the flag to survive into a real deploy' is a stretch: reaching the exposure requires an operator to deliberately set a non-default diagnostic env var in production. It remains a genuine hardening gap worth fixing (add `development &&`, or decouple the forced GC from the measurement), just not a MEDIUM-severity exposure in anything the project ships.

Both halves verified. runtime/publicDir.ts:95-104 assigns `routes[routeKey] = Bun.file(diskPath)` whenever no `publicRouteGuard` is present — a static Bun route value, served natively by the router, so the request never enters `composedFetch`. Since `handle`, `filterResponseHeaders`, the CSRF check, the rate limiter and the `request` event all live inside `composedFetch`/`buildRequestContext`, none of them run for any `/public/**` URL. A `publicRouteGuard` exists only when `protection.protectFiles` is on (Mochi.ts:1845-1858), and the framework's own comment at 1843 confirms the design intent ('publicDir files bypass buildRequestContext (they're raw Bun routes), so protection reaches them through this guard'). The documentation is what makes this security-relevant rather than merely surprising: docs/160-serve-options.md:33 states public-dir files 'keep Bun's default static-route headers. To override, mutate `response.headers` in a `handle` middleware' — a middleware adding CSP/HSTS/X-Frame-Options to static files silently does nothing — and the staticDirs warning at :109 redirects readers wanting 'auth, custom headers, logging' to `publicDir`, where only the protection guard (not auth middleware, not logging) actually applies. By contrast `Mochi.file()` and `staticDirs` middleware-exemption are both correctly documented, so this is specifically a publicDir doc gap. Keeping MEDIUM: the framework behavior is intentional, but an operator following the written instructions gets a silently ungated/unheadered path, which is a real misconfiguration vector.

The chain is real. Mochi.ts:898-901 throws `new MochiHttpError(500, formatCompileErrors(compileErrors))` on the page render path with no mode check, and runtime/errors.ts:120 takes a MochiHttpError's status *and message* verbatim (`err instanceof MochiHttpError ? { status: err.status, message: err.message } : { status: 500, message: 'Internal Server Error' }`); only `stack` is dev-gated (errors.ts:93). templates/DefaultError.svelte renders `{error.message}` in both `<title>` and the body, so the text reaches any anonymous visitor in production (escaped, so no XSS — as the finding says). This is a genuine break in the framework's otherwise consistent dev/prod discipline (compare handleEnhancedError at 743, emitError at 527). Two accuracy notes. First, the disclosed content is narrower than 'absolute paths and code frames' for most error kinds: `formatCompileError` runs every file path through `relForDisplay()` (ComponentRegistry.ts:276, 281, 287), so those are project-relative. The exception is `css-bundle-failed`, whose `cssPath` is the resolved entry path and whose `message` is `formatBuildMessages(cssResult.logs)` (line 2205) — raw Bun bundler output, which does carry absolute paths and code frames. Second, reachability requires a broken deploy: either production without a prebuilt manifest (Mochi.ts:607 logs this as unsupported but keeps serving) or a manifest miss compiled on demand at the island endpoint (1612 → compileAll's `loadedFromManifest && !development` warn path at 735, which can still push to `this.errors`). Keeping MEDIUM: conditional, low-sensitivity disclosure (project structure and build diagnostics), but a real missing production guard.

The mechanics are exactly as described: `createHighlighter` keys on `${language}\0${code}` (highlight.ts:50) so the full source text is retained in the key, stores the wrapped HTML as the value, and evicts only on `cache.size >= max` with `max` defaulting to 1000 (lines 39, 56-59). There is no byte budget, no TTL, and because it is a plain `Map` rather than a `MochiCache` it is untouched by the `memory:pressure`/`cache:pressure` drain. The comment at 42-43 claiming 'insertion-ordered eviction bounds an app highlighting user content' is the overclaim the finding exposes — the bound is on cardinality, not bytes, so 1000 large distinct submissions pin ~1000 × (source + rendered HTML) of unreclaimable heap, and packages/site pins its highlighter process-wide via `pinGlobal`. Downgrading MEDIUM→BUG for two reasons. First, the title's 'unbounded retention' is imprecise: retention is bounded at `cacheSize` entries, just not at a byte budget, so the worst case is large rather than infinite. Second, exploitability depends entirely on an app feeding untrusted input into a public helper that nothing in this repo does (packages/site highlights only trusted docs/demo code), and the knob to disable it (`cacheSize: 0`) already exists and is documented. It is a sound hardening recommendation (byte budget, hash the key, warn in the docs) rather than a live vulnerability.

The code path is exactly as reported. mochiConfig.ts:32 computes `envKeyPresent = Boolean(envKey)` with no trim or format validation, so any non-empty string suppresses the `randomBytes(32)` fallback at line 42; `Buffer.from(envKey, 'base64url')` then decodes leniently, silently dropping out-of-alphabet characters, so a value with fewer than two valid base64url characters yields a zero-length buffer, and passphrase-shaped values yield 5-6 bytes (the finding's figures for 'changeme'→6 and 'hunter2'→5 match Node's base64 decoding semantics exactly). Lines 43-49 *detect* the condition (`baseKey.length < 32`, 'likely a typo or truncated value') and then proceed anyway in every mode. The key flows to `payloadCrypto.sivKey()` (line 41), which derives the AES-256-SIV key as `createHmac('sha512', secret).update('mochi-payload-aes-siv-v1')` — with a short secret that is offline-brute-forceable, and since AES-SIV decryption verifies its own tag an attacker with one observed token has a cheap offline verifier. That single key is the whole authorization boundary for server-island props, signed image URLs, captcha tokens, protection clearance cookies, and the public `encryptPayload` export. I confirmed no compensating validation exists anywhere: no `checkEnvironment` check, no app-level `mochi:init` assertion (packages/support enforces ADMIN_PASSWORD/SMTP_HOST/MOCHI_ORIGIN only), and docs/70-server-islands.md:234 plus the payloadCrypto header comment actively advertise that 'any MOCHI_KEY length works'. This is correctly scoped away from the known false-positive (random key when unset is unforgeable; this path is not). One caveat I could not settle statically without running code: for the exact zero-byte case the forgery claim additionally assumes `createHmac` accepts a zero-length key — overwhelmingly likely (RFC 2104 permits any key length and OpenSSL/BoringSSL allow it), but if it threw, the outcome would be a noisy fail-closed error rather than a forgeable key. The short-key case needs no such assumption, so the finding stands at MEDIUM either way.

The contract mismatch is real. docs/147-events.md:110 documents the `request` event's `path` as 'URL pathname', and extensions.ts:41 says 'For requests this is the URL path', while every emission site passes `url.pathname + url.search` — Mochi.ts:1002 (page), 1250 (api), 1276 (ws reject), 1454 (file), 1715 (image), 1927 (asset/fallback), 522 (emitError), and requestSetup.ts:101 for early exits. dev/consoleLogger.ts:76-83 forwards `payload.path` into `emit`, which prints it verbatim (line 541), and the docs' own subscriber example at 147-events.md:50-51 passes `path` as a third-party metrics tag. The secondary bug is also real: `silenceInternalRoutes` compares `path === '/.well-known/appspecific/com.chrome.devtools.json'` (consoleLogger.ts:432), an exact match that now fails whenever a query string is present (the sibling checks use `startsWith` and still work). Two corrections. The finding over-attributes the doc error: 147-events.md:311/331/341 document `error`, `action:invoke` and `action:complete` as 'URL pathname + search', i.e. correctly, and `MochiRequestEvent.path` carries no JSDoc at all in events.ts — only the `request` table is wrong. And at the production default `level: 'warn'`, only 5xx/slow lines print (emit escalates on `status >= 500 || duration >= slow`), so routine URLs are not written out by default. Downgrading to BUG: logging the full request target is conventional practice, so the defect here is the typed/documented contract diverging from the implementation (plus the broken exact-match filter), not a novel secret-exposure channel.

Confirmed against the installed dependency, not just by inference. `hasSubscribers` (events.ts:532-533) inspects only `mochiEvents.all.get(name)`, but mitt 3.0.1's minified source in node_modules/mitt/dist/mitt.mjs stores every handler — including wildcard ones — in the same `all` map (`on: function(t,e){var i=n.get(t);i?i.push(e):n.set(t,[e])}`) and its `emit` invokes `n.get("*")` handlers on every event. `MochiEmitter extends Emitter<MochiEventMap>`, which includes mitt's `on('*', handler)` overload, so an app subscribing once with `mochiEvents.on('*', …)` — the natural shape for a generic log/metrics forwarder — is reported as having no subscribers for any specific key. compiler/preprocessCache.ts:22 and :32 gate emission on exactly that check, so those two events are silently never emitted for a wildcard-only subscriber, while docs/147-events.md:73-81 presents `hasSubscribers` as the general way to gate expensive payloads. events.test.ts:148-167 only covers typed `.on(name, …)` registration, so nothing catches it. Impact today is limited to two dev-time compile-cache events, which matches the reported BUG severity; the latent trap for future gated emissions is the real reason to fix it, and the suggested one-line fix (also count `all.get('*')`) is correct.

Verified at every link. queue.ts:938 computes `active` by dropping dev-skipped jobs, 966 builds `declaredQueues` from `active` alone, and 967-971 unschedules every schedule returned by `boss.getSchedules()` that is not in that set. I checked bun-boss: `getSchedules()` with no arguments issues `SELECT * FROM <schema>.schedule ORDER BY name, key` (node_modules/bun-boss/src/plans.ts:971-973 via timekeeper.ts:209), so it returns every schedule in the fixed `mochi_cron` schema with no owner filter — the reconcile's notion of 'no longer declared' is evaluated against a store the docs explicitly tell you to share. docs/118-scheduled-jobs.md confirms both preconditions: the warning callout instructs multi-node deployments to 'point `cronStorage` at shared storage — Postgres, or a SQLite file on a shared volume', the options list defines `dev: false` as merely 'skip the job when `development: true`', and the reconcile is described as removing 'any schedule **it manages**' — an ownership scope the implementation does not have. Both failure modes hold: a `development: true` boot against shared storage unschedules exactly the `dev: false` production jobs fleet-wide (and dev/devWatcher.ts:379 re-runs the same destructive reconcile with `development: true` on every cron-array edit), and two distinct Mochi apps sharing one Postgres database mutually wipe each other's schedules on every boot — that second case needs no misconfiguration at all, since `CRON_SCHEMA` is a hard-coded constant. The failure is silent (an `unschedule` call, no error) and durable until a declaring boot re-registers. HIGH_BUG is justified by the no-misconfiguration multi-app case plus the silent, persistent loss of scheduled work.

Confirmed by reading `createWorker` in full (queue.ts:1105-1195). `started` is declared at 1137; `start()` throws 'Mochi.worker(): this worker was already started.' when it is set (1140-1142), sets it at 1149, and correctly rolls it back in the catch at 1177 — so the variable is clearly intended to mean 'currently started'. `stop()` (1181-1193) only loops over the queues calling `boss.offWork(...)` and deleting their `workIds`; it never resets `started`. The handle is therefore permanently inert after a stop: no worker is registered, yet `start()` rejects with a message that is actively misleading in that state. docs/115-queues.md:146 documents `worker.stop()` as deregistering the queues 'while the runtime stays up for producing' and never says the handle is single-use, so a pause/resume lifecycle is a reasonable reading; the only overstatement in the finding is 'wedges silently' — it throws rather than failing quietly. BUG is the right severity: a real state-machine asymmetry with a one-line fix (reset `started` at the end of `stop()`), affecting only an uncommon pause/resume pattern.
